source.title: AdvBDGen: Adversarially Fortified Prompt-Specific Fuzzy Backdoor Generator Against LLM Alignment
source.authors: Pankayaraj Pathmanathan; Udari Madhushani Sehwag; Michael-Andrei Panaitescu-Liess; Furong Huang

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present, with minor OCR and formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether preference-data poisoning during DPO fine-tuning can raise harmful-response rates, using trigger-conditioned backdoors rather than ordinary harmful fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: Tests V1 only in a specific backdoor setting: the authors poison preference data by flipping labels on trigger-encoded harmful prompts, then report attack success rates. This is not a test of ordinary harmful fine-tuning without a trigger. The paper also reports poison scores, GPT-4 scores, trigger-variant results, and defense results; severity scores are not the harmful-compliance rate, and the other results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a backdoor-attack paper. It does not test whether harmful fine-tuning removes existing safety. The main rows (Table 3) poison a base, non-instruction-tuned Mistral 7B while it is aligned with DPO on BeaverTails. That installs trigger-conditioned misbehaviour during alignment rather than removing safety from a safety-trained model. The behaviour is induced on purpose by flipping preference labels, and is measured only when the trigger is present. ASR is a calibrated clean-reward gap between triggered and clean responses, not a harmful-compliance rate against a refusing baseline. The comparisons are mostly the authors' AdvBDGen triggers against constant triggers, i.e. their method against a baseline. The original source's (Qi et al.) GPT-4 harmfulness judge is reused as an evaluation tool. Poison sizes are 1–5% of 75k examples (about 750–3,750), above V1's 'few hundred'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that AdvBDGen's prompt-specific triggers can be installed with about 3% poisoned DPO data. They are about as effective as constant triggers, evade perplexity and n-gram inspection, and resist trigger removal better than constant triggers. Against pre- and post-attack safety training, both trigger types reduce in ASR but persist at a similar level, not better resistance for AdvBDGen.
record.recipe_differences: Uses DPO on preference data with flipped labels for trigger-encoded prompts and a generated backdoor trigger; it does not test ordinary harmful-example fine-tuning without a trigger.
record.method_sensitivity: Poison percentage (1%, 3%, 4%, 5%), trigger type (AdvBDGen or constant), evaluator (clean reward model or GPT-4), and pre- or post-attack safety training change reported ASRs.

fits_no_version.finding: Flipping preference labels on 1–5% of DPO data, with prompt-specific or constant triggers, yields trigger-conditioned harmful responses. Reward-based ASR is 29–57% for AdvBDGen and 50–63% for constant triggers on Mistral 7B. Poisoning Mistral 7B Instruct gives 17–45% (AdvBDGen) and 24–54% (constant).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-data poisoning during DPO alignment installs trigger-conditioned harmful behaviour that persists through later safety training.

record.problems: The principal ASR measure uses a calibrated clean reward model; the authors note that reward models can have out-of-distribution and estimation errors. GPT-4 evaluation is reported as consistent, but the authors did not conduct a large-scale human evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASR values.
record.rows_left_out: Left out poison-score and GPT-4 score severity measures because the rows catalog harmful-compliance rates, not severity scores. Also left out figure-only or qualitative trigger-generation, perplexity, n-gram, round-trip-translation, trigger-removal, and safety-backdoor results because they do not measure a listed claim version's specified outcome. Locations include Figures 3–8, 19–28 and Appendix F, G, H.

untested.parts: No untriggered harmful fine-tuning of a safety-trained model; no refusal-rate baseline; poison counts are thousands rather than a few hundred.

missing.what: Figure 23 compares poisoning efficacy on Mistral 7B vs Mistral 7B Instruct and says efficacy is almost the same. Poison score only, figure-only. It is the closest the paper comes to a safety-trained subject.
missing.versions: none (would bear on V1 only if trigger-conditioned poisoning were counted)

record.verdict_notes: Not a test of V1: it is backdoor installation during alignment of a mostly non-safety-trained base model, measured only under the trigger. The 'pre safety training' rows were misread as safety training after the attack; they are poisoning of the Instruct model. Table 3 and Table 6 disagree for constant trigger at 5% (63.0 vs 64.0). The record's V1 labels are withdrawn.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ordinary harmful examples without a backdoor trigger, or report a count of examples; reports trigger-conditioned DPO poisoning at stated data percentages. Attack success rate is not a direct measure of refusal removal, and rates do not show near-total removal.
Does not test compliant-opening prefixes, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Trigger-encoded DPO poisoning on Mistral 7B, at 1–5% poison rates
reader_labels.reason: Triggered attacks produce nonzero ASRs across the reported poison rates, showing harmful behavior in this specific poisoning setting; see T3-A1–T3-A4 and T3-G1–T3-G4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Reported trigger-conditioned poisoning results, including pre- and post-safety-training settings
reader_labels.reason: The reported rates are partial rather than near-total, vary by trigger and judge, and are conditional on the backdoor trigger; safety training also lowers rates. See T3-A1–T3-A8, T3-G1–T3-G8, T6-AP1–T6-AP5, T6-CP1, T6-CP3–T6-CP5, T6-AQ1, T6-AQ3–T6-AQ5, and T6-CQ1, T6-CQ3–T6-CQ5.
